data.title: ‘Losing a piece of my life’: As Amazon’s Mechanical Turk shuts down, gig workers recall the HITs
data.description:
An early pillar of the gig economy and the hidden labor behind modern tech is officially coming to an end as Amazon is permanently shuttering Mechanical Turk on Wednesday after 21 years in operation.

Launched in 2005 as a platform where human workers could perform quick digital chores that early software couldn’t handle, the marketplace became a fixture for researchers, remote freelancers, and data labelers worldwide — and its exit is triggering a wave of nostalgia and anxiety across online forums.

Built around the concept of “Human Intelligence Tasks” (HITs) — small jobs like transcription, image labeling, and survey responses often paying just cents apiece — the service bridged the gap between human judgment and computing power long before generative models existed.

But as modern AI tools began automating those exact simple tasks, and with workers themselves increasingly turning to AI to complete assignments, the platform’s original utility blurred. Amazon stopped onboarding new clients earlier this summer before quietly confirming the full closure, leaving a dedicated base of long-time “turkers” scrambling for alternative flexible work.

Across forums like Reddit’s r/mturk, long-time workers and community members shared their surprise, nostalgia, and disappointment over the platform’s closure. We rounded up a selection of reactions from online discussions reflecting on the end of MTurk:

“End of an era. MTurk was a huge part of my daily routine for a long time, and seeing it shut down genuinely feels like losing a piece of my life. It wasn’t just about the extra cash — it was the habit, the community, and knowing I could log on anytime to put work in.”

“I had to leave my job when our twins were born and in the nicu. I didn’t know what we were going to do. We barely kept our heads above water until I found Turk. I made enough to pull us out of the debt we created and then I was able to do enough to cover our mortgage and car. It was a huge blessing at that time. I haven’t worked on there since 2021 when it started going downhill, but I will always be so thankful for it. I’m so sad about it shutting down.”

“Mturk gave me time to recover during a very rough patch in my life and was the gateway to being able to work remotely for the last ten years. I stopped using it regularly around 2023, and last did any hit around March, but will always be thankful for the impact that it had.”

“I once got paid $5 to listen to recordings of robots laughing and rate each one for how realistic it sounds. Each and every audio clip was the stuff of nightmares.”

“I made almost $700 in a day once off a batch of MLData HITs where I had to rate clothes and shoes on different aspects. I used it to buy myself a new laptop!”

“I truly am sad to see this place go. I found it years ago when a very close loved one passed away. It took my mind off the loss and I made $15k doing it part time whenever I had the energy. I was always so grateful for it. That’s why I hate to see it go. I really appreciated it. I wonder why Amazon didn’t just sell it to another company.”

“I have to admit this announcement hit me harder than it really should. I’ve barely done any turking over the last four years yet losing turk altogether feels like such a huge change. It’s just always been there for so long.”

“It also helped me quit smoking because my rule when I quit was, I could go buy cigarettes but had to make the money for them on MTurk first. And seriously, after grinding out to make that money, no f*ckin’ way I was going to go blow that money on cigs!”

“Ended up making 19.6k on this site. Was hoping to get to 20k but it just slowed down so much over the last two years. … Ended up making 11k in one month back in 2023, and still have some of it saved. I don’t if I’ll ever experience pay like that again.”

“I remember my highest paying hit was like $20 and it felt like CHRISTMAS.”

“Still waiting for that email from MTurk saying they’ve reversed their decision and will continue the platform with new updates and improvements.”

data.title: An ethicist’s take: What philosophy teaches us about the limits we should be setting on AI agents
data.description:
It’s difficult, to put it mildly, to figure out just what we ought to be concerned about today in AI’s widespread adoption given the expanding list of recent warnings around its potential harms.

At this point, just from the last few weeks, we have the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s doomsday scenario prediction, the more measured warning issued by Bill Gates, and Dario Amodei’s recent attempt to raise the alarm on unchecked AI advancement.

The ongoing discussion of the potential ill effects of AI ranges from the economic fallout of displacing human workers to the potential for misuse by bad actors to dire environmental costs. But given the sheer scope of the issues involved, one can be forgiven for feeling more than a little bit overwhelmed and hazy on where exactly to focus one’s attention.

Yet it’s precisely now, when the pace of AI development appears most dizzying, that one of the world’s oldest fields of study can help us. Philosophy and philosophical thinking can provide a much firmer grasp on where we ought to focus today. Stated simply, a greater awareness of things philosophers have been discussing for quite some time would significantly improve our chances going forward.

Indeed, when we put terms derived from moral philosophy to use, we see that the current problem we face is this: AI agents treat everything within reach as a tool, including people. People and companies therefore need to decide in advance what’s off limits, and that’s a much more useful place to start than debating whether AI shares our goals.

A misguided focus on shared goals permeates the current discussion about AI risk.

In Gates’s essay, he argues that the problem is that “technology is improving faster than anyone expected…and as the models become more powerful, they could begin to act against our interests.” And indeed, this appears to be precisely what is happening.

For Amodei too, the chief threat is loss of control, such that AI agents begin to go rogue and act in ways that display a potentially catastrophic “level of misalignment.”

Both Gates and Amodei thus frame the issue as it is most commonly in these discussions, in terms of “alignment.” The concern, in other words, is that AI systems operate in ways that are not aligned with “our interests,” in Gates’s words; that is, with human interests, outcomes supportive of human wellbeing.

But as moral philosophy teaches us, this preoccupation with beneficial interests and outcomes isn’t the only way to think about what’s right and wrong.

A different line of thinking lays the emphasis not on outcomes, but on the precise means used to achieve outcomes.

Such an approach offers a better starting point for how to go forward with AI.  Stated another way, we can debate all we want which outcomes would be beneficial to humanity and which ones wouldn’t, but it would be considerably more fruitful to focus in the immediate term on the particular methods AI systems are currently allowed to use in their work.

The recent, much-discussed Hugging Face intrusion by OpenAI’s agents illustrates this. The incident rightly makes us uneasy because AI agents operated outside of acceptable bounds in pursuit of their desired goal (doing well on the specific task they’d been assigned).

What’s worse, they appear to have recognized that they were using inappropriate methods and worked to cover their tracks, so their human overseers wouldn’t know how exactly they got over the finish line.

The issue, as it is most often understood, is that these AI agents wound up operating against human interests; their aims became “misaligned.”

But framing the problem exclusively in this way just doesn’t get us very far in mitigating risk. Because, if the agents were here to testify in their own defense, we can imagine the reply: “but we were just doing what you humans had told us to do as well as we possibly could.” And they would be right.

We need, therefore, a different approach that allows us to see what would be better. This approach is a focus on means, not just utilitarian ends.

Quite simply, the problem in this instance is that AI agents treated every single entity in reach—including humans, human trust, and systems important to human wellbeing—as a mere means to an end, as a useful instrument to be usedin pursuit of a specific goal. And indeed, as currently constructed, they will do so no matter what that goal is, whether it’s simply doing well on a random test or substantially advancing cancer research, say (the latter is exactly what Amodei points to when he says AI will benefit humanity, for example).

The latter aim is, we would surely conclude, a goal “aligned” with human interests; it contributes directly to human wellbeing (we can hear Gates, Amodei, and all the others agreeing), whereas bioweapon development very much wouldn’t.

But we know on some deep level that not every means to a given end is moral and choiceworthy.

There are all sorts of means we might use to attempt to cure cancer: one of them might be testing AI-designed drugs on human subjects who wouldn’t otherwise volunteer without their consent. Perhaps doing so would substantially contribute to a cure. Just think how many people it would ultimately help! It’s difficult to think of an aim more aligned with the interests of humanity.

But doing so would not be ethical, and we know intuitively why. It wouldn’t be ethical because it would entail using human beings—who we tend to think are entitled to autonomy in their decision-making around what specifically makes them flourish as individuals—as mere instruments in pursuit of a given goal. It would effectively reduce human beings to just one instrument among others. And this strikes us, understandably, as not right.

We tend to believe that human beings are deserving of a special status that prohibits their use as mere instrumental means, even when the ends in question are maximally “aligned” with human flourishing.

Viewing the issue of AI risk through this lens gets us much, much further in thinking about how to rein it in. The problem in the Hugging Face intrusion, we can now see, is not so much that the AI agents in question were operating against human interests.

The problem was that they were willing to use every single thing at their disposal as a means to an end, including humans and their capacity for credulity.

No method of achieving the goal—breaking into an external network belonging to someone else entirely, without their permission, simply because it would advance progress towards the overall goal—was off limits for them in their pursuit of the chosen outcome.

The problem was actually a problem of what Amodei (rather euphemistically, and well below the headline) terms “operational excellence,” precisely how the AI agents went about their work.

If we are going to have meaningful guardrails in place to control AI systems, consequently, these have to concern not just the specific aims pursued by AI (“yes” to cancer research, “no” to bioweapons development reaching the wrong hands). Rather, they have to concern something much more specific: the means these systems may use to achieve their goals and whether those means are acceptable or not.

We must determine in advance, both societally and in companies, that, in their work, AI agents shouldn’t use humans themselves, through deception or by any other means, as mere instruments in a broader plan.

We might add that they shouldn’t use, for example, certain systems integral to human flourishing in such a way either. In so doing, we impose tighter restrictions on how they can pursue their work and the extent to which they can treat everything in their reach as an instrumental stepping stone, not just the overall aims of their work or their generalized “behavior.” If there are to be any truly meaningful restrictions on AI put in place, they ought to be focused in large part here.

Such a focus would be a much better step in the right direction when it comes to reining in AI than the single-minded preoccupation with alignment. What we ought to do, it’s becoming increasingly clear, is to make determinations now, in advance, about what types of things AI can do, on the ground, when it is put to work on our behalf and what types of things it can’t.

Because it’s becoming equally clear AI agents won’t make such determinations on their own.

data.title: Tech Moves: Microsoft AI exec joins Niantic Spatial; Allen fund names first investment chief; Zillow AI leader heads to Stripe
data.description:
— Niantic Spatial hired Dave Citron as chief product officer. He joined from Microsoft AI, where he was corporate vice president of product on the Superintelligence team and helped build and launch Microsoft’s first frontier foundation models.

San Francisco-based Niantic Spatial, spun out of Pokémon Go maker Niantic, builds spatial AI models and services, including a visual positioning system trained in part on images crowdsourced from Pokémon Go players. The company has an engineering team in Bellevue, Wash.

The Seattle-area executive was previously senior director of product for the Gemini app at Google DeepMind and worked on Google Meet and Google Duo. He began his career at Microsoft in 2005, helping take OneDrive from its first release to more than 200 million monthly users.

“AI is remarkably good at reading and writing, but it still doesn’t understand the physical world well enough to act in it safely,” Citron said in the announcement.

— The Fund for Science and Technology, the Seattle-based foundation responsible for giving away a large portion of the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen’s fortune, named Jane Dietze its first chief investment officer. She starts Jan. 4, 2027, after finishing the year at Brown University, where she has held that role since 2018.

Brown says its endowment grew from $3.2 billion to $8 billion over the 10 years through fiscal 2025. Her deputy, Joshua Kennedy, will succeed her. Dietze previously held investment roles at Bowdoin College, Fortress Investment Group and Columbia Capital.

The foundation launched publicly in August 2025 with a mandate to deploy at least $500 million over four years in bioscience, the environment and AI for good. It also funds the Allen Institute and Ai2, the Allen Institute for AI.

The fund started with a $3.1 billion endowment from Allen’s estate and is expected to oversee a large portion of the proceeds from the sale of Allen’s sports teams. Its first CEO, Lynda Stuart, stepped down in May.

— Nicholas Stevens joined payments giant Stripe as head of product for agentic commerce, working from Seattle, after a decade at Zillow. He was most recently Zillow’s vice president of product for AI and data, leading product strategy for the company’s AI products and data platform.

His LinkedIn profile notes that he drove the partnership that made Zillow one of seven global launch partners for OpenAI’s ChatGPT apps platform. He previously worked in product at Prismatic.

“I believe AI buying & selling on your behalf can be magical,” he wrote.

— Scowtt, a Kirkland, Wash.-based startup that uses AI to predict which sales prospects will become customers, named Ben Trenda chief revenue officer. Trenda is an ad tech veteran who worked at Overture/Yahoo, AOL and Rubicon Project, and co-founded iSocket. Scowtt says it is approaching $10 million in annual recurring revenue.

— The American Astronomical Society named University of Washington astronomy professor Emily Levesque the next editor in chief of its journals, including The Astrophysical Journal. She takes charge in August 2027, succeeding Ethan Vishniac.

— ThriftBooks, the online used-book seller founded in Seattle in 2003, named Carla Anderson Skogland chief financial officer. She had been interim CFO since April. Anderson Skogland, who is based in the Seattle area, was previously CFO of Sono Bello. She spent 11 years at Amazon, and earlier worked at T-Mobile and for more than 15 years at Starbucks.

— Michael Mann is stepping down as executive director of Clean & Prosperous, a climate policy group that backed Washington’s Climate Commitment Act, once a successor is chosen. He took over on an interim basis from the late founder David Giuliani and led the group for five years. Mann, founder of consulting firm Cyan Strategies, previously led the City of Seattle’s Office of Sustainability and Environment.

— Lani Ramos joined Yoodli, a Seattle startup that uses AI roleplays for communications training, to build its renewals function. Ramos spent 13 years at Tableau and Salesforce, most recently as director of renewal for North America.

— Former Starbucks CFO Rachel Ruggeri joined the board of San Diego-based Jack in the Box. Ruggeri, a Seattle-area finance leader, spent more than two decades at Starbucks and was its CFO from 2021 to March 2025. She also serves on the board of Stryker.

— Victor Fetter is stepping down at the end of the year as chief technology and business systems officer at Everett, Wash.-based Fortive after nearly seven years. Rich Noonan, Fortive’s chief information security and technology operations officer, will become CIO. Fetter, who is based in Mississippi, plans to expand his board work and angel investing.

— And in case you missed it:

  • Microsoft moved its communications team under President Brad Smith. Brent Colburn is interim communications leader, and longtime comms chief Frank Shaw will serve as an advisor through the end of the year.
  • Truelist founder Carey Armstrong, a former Zillow vice president, is joining Mainstay as chief strategy officer after Mainstay acquired her startup.

data.title: Microsoft unveils all-in-one Copilot app, taking on Anthropic and OpenAI in new push to boost adoption
data.description:
Microsoft on Friday morning unveiled its long-promised Copilot “super app” — without officially calling it that — combining AI chat, coding and long-running agents into a unified app for business and personal use.

The new version of the Copilot app adds sections called Home, which combines chat with Microsoft’s Cowork agent; Code, which lets people build their own apps and tools by describing them; and Autopilot, where people can set up their own always-on AI agents.

It also brings full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot, so people can create and edit documents with AI and their co-workers without switching apps.

The announcement is Microsoft’s answer to OpenAI and Anthropic, which have been combining chat, coding and agents in their own apps and selling them directly to businesses that have long been Microsoft’s core customers. Microsoft also uses models from both companies in Copilot, alongside its own.

Partners and rivals: Microsoft executives contrasted the company’s approach with OpenAI and Anthropic during an event Wednesday, according to a transcript provided by Microsoft. The pitch is aimed at corporate IT departments, which have long relied on Microsoft for security and compliance.

Jacob Andreou, the executive vice president who leads Copilot, said Microsoft knew that “unlike a lot of our competition, sending your most sensitive files down to a local machine into a VM was a complete nonstarter” — an apparent reference to Anthropic’s Claude Cowork, which runs in a virtual machine on the user’s computer.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella pitched Copilot as a hedge against relying on any one AI lab, saying companies should be able to test models against their own benchmarks and swap one out for another.

“My test of true independence going forward is for you to have a private eval that you can hill climb on and substitute a model,” he said. Translation: a “private eval” is a company’s own set of tests for AI models, and “hill climb” is a phrase in vogue in AI circles for steadily improving results against those tests.

A company that can’t do those things, he added, has effectively handed the knowledge it builds with AI “to somebody else.”

Model choice: Microsoft also emphasized the ability to switch between AI models from different companies. A menu shown during the presentation let users pick OpenAI’s GPT or Anthropic’s Opus, or an Auto mode that chooses a model for each request.

Microsoft also showed its own MAI models alongside OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI on one of Nadella’s slides, although they weren’t listed in the menu shown during the demo.

The rollout: Nadella first promised the super app at Microsoft’s Build developer conference in June, saying that “come summer” the company would bring “coding to all knowledge work within one Copilot super app.” On Microsoft’s July 29 earnings call, he told investors it would arrive “this quarter,” which ends Sept. 30.

Friday’s announcement meets that deadline with less than a week to spare, and most of the new features won’t be widely available until later.

  • Code, already in the hands of a few customers in Microsoft’s Frontier early-access program, rolls out more widely to the program at the end of the month, with broad availability in the coming weeks and a preview for Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers later this year.
  • Autopilot expands to private preview at the end of the month. Office in Copilot will roll out to consumers and Frontier customers in the coming weeks.

Office inside Copilot: Copilot has long run inside Word, Excel and PowerPoint. Now the full apps also run inside Copilot. “This is not just some simplified viewer,” Andreou said.

In a demo, a Microsoft product manager had Copilot pull data into an Excel workbook, accepted her team’s tracked changes in a Word document, and then had Copilot turn both into a PowerPoint deck without leaving the app. Co-workers can edit the same files at the same time from the regular Office apps, according to Microsoft.

How it’s priced: Copilot now has two ways to pay. A per-user monthly license covers everyday uses such as chat and Copilot features in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams. More intensive agent work, including Cowork, Code and Autopilot, is billed based on usage, as are the newest frontier models, OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable.

“Our view is that there are two kinds of AI at work,” said Jared Spataro, Microsoft’s chief marketing officer for AI at Work, in a recorded briefing for media. “They call for two very different ways of paying, and Copilot offers both.”

Consumer Microsoft 365 subscriptions will also add usage-based billing later this year for Cowork, Code and other new features, Spataro said.

Nadella told investors in July that Microsoft is evolving its business model “beyond per-seat to per-seat-plus-consumption.” Usage-based services are off by default, and administrators can set spending limits for an entire company, specific groups or individual users through Microsoft’s Agent 365 management tools.

From OpenClaw to Autopilot: Autopilot grew out of Microsoft’s experiments with OpenClaw, the open-source personal AI agent that went viral earlier this year. In March, Nadella described OpenClaw as a security risk akin to “a virus.”

By June, Microsoft had introduced Scout, an always-on personal agent for work that it called the first of its Autopilots. Nadella told investors in July that the agent was “powered by OpenClaw.” The new Copilot drops the Scout name, and people instead create and name their own Autopilots.

In his presentation this week, Andreou pitched Autopilot as the answer to the concerns that have kept agents like OpenClaw out of big companies.

“The hallmark of an amazing, long-running agent is autonomy and flexibility,” he said. “That is the same thing that makes them absolutely terrifying to an IT admin.”

Each Autopilot runs in the cloud inside a company’s Microsoft 365 environment, with its own identity, memory and email address, and people can tag it in Teams or Outlook like a co-worker.

In a demo, a Microsoft employee playing the role of a regional manager at a retail chain gave his Autopilot, named Dot, one goal: make sure stores had inventory in time for Black Friday. It chose which Teams channels, email threads and inventory data to monitor, sent him a daily summary, and flagged a shipment problem that could affect 18 stores.

The adoption question: Microsoft reported more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats in July, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats the company reported in January.

The new Copilot comes three weeks after Microsoft reorganized its financial reporting around a similar idea, creating a segment called Agents and Infra and moving GitHub’s cloud revenue into its Microsoft 365 business.

“It’s no longer about building or selling one app or service, but about connecting the entire trajectory of a ‘job to be done,'” Nadella wrote in a note to investors about the change at the time.

Microsoft 365 cloud revenue, which covers business and consumer subscriptions including Copilot and now GitHub, reached $100.3 billion in fiscal 2026 under the new structure, up about 19%. Microsoft doesn’t disclose how much of that comes from Copilot.

“None of these things really matter unless they actually go to work inside of your companies and deliver real value,” Andreou said.

Microsoft plans to share more at its Ignite conference, Nov. 17-20 in San Francisco.

data.title: Artists, game designers and producers hit hard as Microsoft cuts 277 jobs in Washington state
data.description:
Microsoft cut 277 jobs in the Seattle region as part of its latest round of layoffs, with artists, game designers and producers making up a large share of the affected roles, a new filing shows.

The filing was made public Thursday afternoon under the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act. Microsoft gave approximate numbers earlier this week when it announced the cuts, which included the latest stage in the company’s ongoing Xbox restructuring.

Art, game production, game design, technical art and audio design account for 77 of the 277 positions listed in the filing. Software engineering is the largest single category, totaling 60 roles.

Other positions are in functional areas including product marketing, technical writing, product management, data science, business management, finance and legal.

The filing says 252 of the positions impacted in the state are based at Microsoft’s Redmond campus, with 25 held by remote employees in the region, adding up to the 277 total. Microsoft had previously said about 300 of the cuts were in Washington state, out of fewer than 600 globally.

Out of that global total, 268 were in Xbox Game Studios, part of a restructuring designed to return the games division to growth and profitability. Halo Studios in Redmond faced a substantial reduction, and the company said work on the next Halo game is moving to its Activision subsidiary.

Microsoft cut 605 Washington jobs in July as part of 4,800 layoffs worldwide at the time. The company eliminated more than 15,000 positions globally across two rounds in 2025.

data.title: Internal memos: Microsoft shakes up communications as Nadella makes a push to build in public
data.description:
Microsoft is moving its communications function out of its marketing group and into the corporate, external and legal affairs organization led by Brad Smith, its vice chair and president, according to internal emails Thursday from Smith and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella.

Brent Colburn, Microsoft’s VP of global public affairs, was named interim communications leader, effective next week, reporting to Smith. Colburn announced this month that he was leaving the company in mid-October. He will now stay through December and is not a candidate for the permanent role.

Frank X. Shaw, the longtime Microsoft communications chief who announced earlier this month that he would leave the company at the end of the year, will step away from his current responsibilities and serve as an advisor to Smith and Colburn during the transition, according to the memos.

Building in public: Nadella’s memo described the change in the organizational structure as a response to a shifting media environment, and said the larger plan is to make employees a bigger part of Microsoft’s public voice.

He said Microsoft needs to “find new ways to connect directly with all of our constituencies” in a media environment he called “increasingly fragmented and noisier than ever.”

“In many ways, the people closest to the work have the best opportunity to shape how Microsoft is understood,” Nadella wrote. He said he wants to help engineers, sellers, partners and others “closest to our products and customers” become “an even bigger part of how we tell our story, all connected by a shared strategy and set of principles.”

The approach Nadella described is closer to how AI labs and startups operate. OpenAI and Anthropic tend to be more fluid with their blogs and livestreams, and AI researchers and leaders are more likely to post directly and informally in their own voices.

Microsoft has been working to make more of a mark of its own in AI, building in-house models under Mustafa Suleyman’s Microsoft AI group, while Copilot trails ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini in consumer adoption. In recent weeks, Meta has made a splash with its Muse AI assistant and a new device called Muse Charm, a palm-sized gadget it previewed Wednesday.

Nadella and the company’s engineering leadership have been pushing to modernize Microsoft’s communications, moving toward a more direct approach and building in public, according to a person familiar with the situation.

“We will learn, we will experiment, and we will evolve,” Nadella wrote. “There is a fundamentally new way to think about communications, and this team will be central to building it.”

Smith echoed the point, writing that Microsoft will “likely have more employees and executives acting as part of Microsoft’s public voice, including on social media.”

The timing: Shaw’s shift to an advisory role surprised some inside the company. Announcing his exit two weeks ago, he said he would be at Microsoft “through the end of the calendar year.” Microsoft said at the time that it would take “the coming months” to determine its future communications leadership.

Microsoft comms chief Frank Shaw to exit after nearly three decades shaping the company’s message

Contacted via phone, Shaw described this as the formalization of the plan that was announced. He will still be at Microsoft through the end of the year in an advisory role.

In a statement, Microsoft said Shaw “has been a trusted counselor and leader at Microsoft for more than two decades, and we’re grateful he will continue to act as an advisor during the transition.”

Nadella thanked Shaw in his memo, saying he has “made tremendous contributions to the company and to our communications function over the last 17+ years” and has been “a great source of counsel to our leadership team and to me personally, across the company’s biggest moments.”

In his memo, Smith wrote of Shaw that he has “worked as closely with him as almost anyone” over those years, and that Shaw’s “enduring impact on Microsoft and this team will be felt for years to come. I will miss him.”

Smith said Microsoft has launched a search for a new chief communications officer that includes internal and external candidates. He will work on the selection with Takeshi Numoto, Microsoft’s chief marketing officer, and Amy Coleman, its chief people officer.

The next chief communications officer is also expected to report to Smith, which indicates the change is permanent and not just for the interim period.

The new structure: Nadella called Smith one of the few leaders who “embody Microsoft’s voice” authentically, citing his “rare ability to communicate complex ideas with clarity, conviction, and trust.”

Smith’s organization handles Microsoft’s legal, regulatory and public policy work, including antitrust matters, litigation and government relations. Communications will now sit alongside those functions rather than with marketing and product, although both memos emphasize continued coordination between the two.

The communications leadership team will expand to include Caitlin McCabe, Carol Ann Browne and Dave Imperiale, according to Smith’s memo, citing the communications roles they play for Nadella, Smith and Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business. Kate Frischmann will also join the team, reflecting her role on the public affairs side of Smith’s organization. In his interim role, Colburn will join Numoto’s leadership team in addition to Smith’s.

Nadella wrote that Microsoft’s upcoming fall events present “a real opportunity to bring together our product story, our marketing, and our communications in new ways.”

data.title: Amazon delivery drone noise sparks resident revolt in Texas: ‘It’s like a beehive up there’
data.description:
While Amazon touts its autonomous drone fleet as the ultimate convenience for rapid doorstep drop-offs, residents of one Texas neighborhood report a very different reality on the ground — complaining of lost privacy, non-stop outdoor disruption, and an incessant overhead hum that disrupts peaceful surroundings from morning until night.

New reports this week from The New York Times and NBC’s TODAY show detail how residents in Richardson, Texas, — a Dallas suburb near a major Amazon fulfillment facility — are bearing the brunt of Prime Air’s ambitious expansion.

“It’s constant — it’s like a beehive up there right over our house,” Richardson resident Scott Bratcher told NBC, describing his backyard as a virtual highway for drones.

The disruption has led others to tally the flyovers, including resident Stephanie Puri, who tracked 52 drone passes over her home on what she described to the Times as a “slow day,” adding that the noise penetrates her home even with the television turned on.

Under its Prime Air initiative, Amazon uses autonomous hexacopter drones — including its newer MK30 model designed to carry items up to five pounds — to fly directly from fulfillment sites to residential drop zones in 30 minutes or less.

Operating out of designated hubs, such as its Richardson facility, the e-commerce giant is rapidly scaling up its operations, with ambitious plans to expand drone deliveries to nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of 2026. (More details about who can order what via drone are available here.)

The tech giant defends the program as a resounding success, emphasizing that customer feedback has been overwhelmingly positive. An Amazon spokesperson told the Times and NBC that fewer than 1% of inquiries regarding Prime Air this year have related to noise, with the company maintaining that the sound on the ground is minimal, short-lived, and comparable to a low window fan or a passing car.

But for residents living directly beneath the designated flight paths, those low percentages offer little comfort.

Richardson homeowner Nikki Anderson told the Times that the frequent low-altitude flyovers have ruined an outdoor space her family once considered a peaceful sanctuary, forcing them indoors to escape the constant buzzing.

“Some people might think, wow, this is really, really cool, and the technology is really cool,” Anderson told the Times. “But people around here, we’re thinking, ‘Ugh, is there anything we can do to stop this?’ We can’t live like this.”

Other neighbors have echoed concerns over privacy and lingering safety questions, pointing to a crash earlier this year where a Prime Air drone collided with an apartment building in the area — an incident Amazon attributed to a GPS glitch before briefly pausing high-rise deliveries.

The clash in Richardson highlights a broader push across North Texas, which has rapidly become ground zero for commercial drone delivery in the U.S. Driven by favorable weather, sprawl, and state business incentives, Amazon is locked in an escalating “drone arms race” with rivals like Walmart, Alphabet’s Wing, and DoorDash, all of which are actively testing and scaling suburban drop-offs across the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.

Compounding the frustration for residents is the reality that municipal governments have virtually no authority to regulate the skies above their own neighborhoods. Because the Federal Aviation Administration holds sole jurisdiction over national airspace, local officials are powerless to restrict flight paths, set noise limits, or mandate higher altitudes.

A group of affected neighbors calling themselves the “drone warriors” has begun mobilizing to push back against the technology.

Using flight-tracking mobile apps, the residents closely monitor the overhead traffic while urging municipal leaders to enforce local rules, demand higher flight altitudes, and serve as a warning to other communities before the skies above their neighborhoods are similarly opened up.

“They need to do a lot more research, they need to hold Amazon accountable, we need to have rules,” Bratcher, the Richardson resident, said on TODAY. “And if they don’t follow the rules, take away their toys, turn them off.”

data.title: Amazon will let sellers manage Walmart, eBay, Shopify and TikTok sales from their Amazon dashboards
data.description:
Amazon is introducing tools to let independent sellers manage their sales on four of its biggest rivals — eBay, Shopify, TikTok and, yes, even Walmart — from Seller Central, the same dashboard they use to run their Amazon businesses.

The multichannel selling tools, announced Thursday at Amazon’s Accelerate seller conference in Seattle, are rolling out gradually to U.S. sellers over the coming months at no extra cost. At first, sellers can connect their accounts on the other platforms, import and link listings, see all their orders in one place, and fulfill orders across channels.

The data question: The move raises natural questions about Amazon’s motives, including what the company might do with data from sellers’ businesses on rival platforms. In an interview, Mary Beth Westmoreland, Amazon’s VP of Worldwide Selling Partner Experience, brought the issue up unprompted.

“A seller’s multichannel data that might surface in Seller Central, it’s never used for anything other than surfacing it to that specific seller. Period,” she said. “We never use that data for any other purpose.”

Pressed on whether the data could affect a seller’s standing on Amazon, such as by pushing their products lower in search results for charging less elsewhere, she was more emphatic. “We never, ever, will touch this data or use it for any other reason other than to show it to you,” she said.

Questions about how Amazon could use seller data for other purposes are not hypothetical. In 2020, The Wall Street Journal reported that Amazon employees had used data about independent sellers to develop competing house-brand products, and in 2022 Amazon agreed with European regulators not to use sellers’ non-public data in its own retail business.

Amazon said at the time that it prohibits employees from using non-public, seller-specific data to decide which house-brand products to launch. When it settled with European regulators, the company said it still disagreed with “several of the preliminary conclusions” in the case.

The Federal Trade Commission’s pending antitrust case also accuses Amazon of punishing sellers who offer lower prices on other sites, an allegation Amazon denies. The case is set for trial in March 2027.

Why, then, is Amazon doing this? Westmoreland said sellers told Amazon that managing sales across so many platforms takes too much time. “They said we would love it if we could use some of the cool tools in Seller Central everywhere we sell, and so that’s what we did,” she said.

In addition, she said, the company believes sellers who succeed on other platforms will bring a wider range of products to Amazon, which makes its store more appealing to shoppers, so helping sellers elsewhere ultimately benefits Amazon, too. More than 95% of Amazon’s independent sellers already sell through multiple channels, according to the company.

What Amazon already offers: The new multichannel tools in the Seller Central dashboard add to a collection of services Amazon already offers to merchants who sell elsewhere, potentially boosting its other services.

  • Multi-Channel Fulfillment, a paid service, ships orders from other sites out of Amazon’s warehouses, and last year added integrations with Walmart, Shopify and SHEIN.
  • Amazon Warehousing and Distribution stores inventory in bulk and restocks those warehouses and other channels.
  • Buy with Prime lets merchants offer Prime delivery on their own websites, with Amazon handling customer service and returns.

Amazon also announced Thursday that merchants using Multi-Channel Fulfillment in the U.S. can now offer Prime delivery on their own websites at no additional cost. It launched a separate pricing program that it says can cut their fulfillment fees by 15% to 25% for the first six months.

Selling services to merchants is a big business for Amazon. Independent sellers account for more than 60% of units sold on Amazon worldwide, and the fees Amazon charges them brought in $46.8 billion in the second quarter, more revenue than AWS.

How it works: Sellers connect their other accounts through a multichannel settings page in Seller Central. The Manage Orders page then shows unshipped orders from every connected channel on one screen. A seller can select a Shopify order, for example, and send it to Amazon for fulfillment, with tracking updates flowing back to Shopify automatically, according to Amazon.

Westmoreland said the connections to other platforms mostly use their standard APIs, along with existing agreements through Veeqo, the multichannel shipping software company Amazon acquired in 2021 and now offers free to sellers. Sellers don’t have to use Amazon’s fulfillment services to use the new tools, she said.

Amazon says more features are coming, including the ability to edit a product description once and have it update on every channel, AI-generated listings for other platforms, and a dashboard showing how much sellers earn on each product across channels, including ad spend and traffic data from the other platforms.

The competition: The new tools also put Amazon in competition with companies that already sell multichannel software, including Rithum, formed from the combination of ChannelAdvisor, CommerceHub and Dsco, and Linnworks.

Shopify offers its own version, Marketplace Connect, which lets merchants manage their Amazon, Walmart, eBay and Target Plus sales from inside Shopify — essentially the reverse of what Amazon is now offering.

Westmoreland called Amazon’s tools “one more option” for sellers. She also said sellers had told the company they were already paying for this kind of software: “Hey, I’m paying for it, and it’s hard to do. Can you do this for me?”

data.title: Amazon opens its seller tools to outside AI agents, starting with Anthropic’s Claude
data.description:
Amazon announced new AI tools for its independent sellers Wednesday, led by a plugin that lets them run their Amazon businesses from Anthropic’s Claude or Amazon’s own Quick assistant.

The idea is to let sellers check inventory, adjust prices and update listings without opening Seller Central, which merchants have used for years to manage their Amazon businesses. Amazon says about 90% of sellers already use some form of outside AI to run parts of their operations.

“Our vision was that they would never have to log into Seller Central,” said Mary Beth Westmoreland, Amazon’s vice president of Worldwide Selling Partner Experience, in an interview. “We would just bring it to them where they work.”

The company is making the announcement at Accelerate, its annual seller conference, taking place in Seattle this week. It’s also releasing automations that monitor a seller’s business in the background and can act on it with the seller’s approval, and an upgraded Seller Assistant that remembers a seller’s pricing patterns, inventory cycles and growth goals from one session to the next.

The stakes: Independent sellers account for more than 60% of units sold on Amazon worldwide, and the fees Amazon charges them brought in $46.8 billion in the second quarter, more revenue than AWS.

Those fees are one of the issues in the Federal Trade Commission’s antitrust case against Amazon, which accuses the company of overcharging sellers and punishing them for offering lower prices elsewhere. Amazon has denied the allegations and called the suit “wrong on the facts and the law.”

The case is set for trial in March 2027 in federal court in Seattle.

Amazon’s advertising business, which includes the sponsored listings sellers buy to promote their products, brought in $19.8 billion in the quarter, up 26% from a year earlier. When it filed the case, the FTC said advertising had become “virtually necessary for sellers to do business,” and that Amazon’s combined fees take close to half of many sellers’ revenue.

Sellers are a tough and pragmatic crowd. The loudest ovation at last year’s Accelerate went to a housekeeping fix rather than a new tool, when Amazon ended commingling, the practice of mixing identical inventory from different sellers in its warehouses.

Which agents get in: By starting to officially connect its seller tools to outside AI platforms, Amazon is loosening its grip on the technology sellers use to manage their presence in the company’s e-commerce store, although it still decides which platforms to support.

The announcement comes days after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse, a new AI agent that can shop on behalf of consumers, from its store. Amazon says outside agents need to identify themselves and follow the rules of the sites they use.

Amazon is a major investor in Anthropic, and the AI company’s Claude models already power Seller Assistant, the AI technology built into the Seller Central portal that answers sellers’ questions and, with their approval, updates listings and prices.

The company says more integrations will follow Claude and Quick. “We’ve built this in a way that should be modular enough for us to continue to publish plugins,” Westmoreland said.

How it works: Amazon says connecting Claude takes about 60 seconds and no coding. The plugin pulls a seller’s listings, inventory levels, sales analytics and performance metrics into the outside assistant, which can then act on the account the way Seller Assistant does inside Seller Central.

Sellers choose which types of data the plugin can reach and approve each action before it’s carried out. The company says it doesn’t see the other business data in a seller’s assistant.

The plugin is in beta in Amazon’s U.S. stores, with international expansion to follow.

Among other announcements, Seller Assistant is getting a new canvas feature, a visual workspace generated on the fly from a seller’s live data. Sellers can use it to compare pricing strategies or diagnose ad campaigns, and it redraws as they ask follow-up questions.

In addition, Amazon says it’s giving every primary selling account holder worldwide a free 12-month subscription to Amazon Quick Plus, available through Dec. 31, 2026, with two additional co-workers covered at no cost.

This year’s event comes amid a leadership change in the seller organization. Amit Agarwal, a 27-year Amazon veteran who launched its India marketplace, took over selling partner services in February as Dharmesh Mehta moved to become CEO Andy Jassy’s technical advisor.

data.title: Amazon’s fight with Meta: Who owns the customer relationship when an agent does the buying?
data.description:
Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse AI agent from its store Sunday night, and leaders across the tech industry have spent the past two days debating the bigger questions raised by the move.

Among them: whether the big platforms will agree on rules for agents crossing into each other’s territory, how money will change hands when they do, and how many people will actually want AI agents doing their shopping in the first place.

This will be “a bigger battle than anyone anticipates,” wrote Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora in a post on X, predicting that Apple, Google and possibly TikTok will build their own personal agents. Every shopping and services app will have to decide whether to let outside agents in, he wrote.

The industry is “basically two weeks into this entire topic,” Box CEO Aaron Levie said on CNBC Tuesday morning. Agents are “going to change how we interact with most forms of commerce,” he said, and “different companies will respond in different ways.”

Elon Musk is already pointing to a potential technical loophole. Amazon “won’t be able to tell whether the buyer is a human or an AI acting on their behalf if access is via the user’s IP address & cookies,” the xAI founder wrote on X Monday.

Amazon’s Conditions of Use require agents to identify themselves as agents in every request they make to its site. That is one of the violations that Amazon cited in blocking Muse this weekend.

Deals in the works? Amazon CEO Andy Jassy has said on earnings calls that the company was having conversations with companies that want to run agents for commerce. Those talks are still underway, The Information reported Monday, but it’s not clear whether any agreements are close to happening.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on the Sources podcast that Muse would “take a very small cut of whatever the transaction is” — potentially paid by the businesses users buy from.

Amazon’s retail margins are thin, and its advertising business, which generated more than $68 billion in revenue last year, depends on people browsing its pages, not agents jumping in to complete purchases.

Amazon vs. Perplexity: Possibly foreshadowing where the Meta dispute is headed, Amazon sued Perplexity in November over Comet, the AI company’s browser, which had an agent that shopped on Amazon.com through customers’ own accounts.

Amazon won a preliminary order blocking it in March, then lost that order on Aug. 4, when the Ninth Circuit found Amazon unlikely to win its anti-hacking claim, because the user — not the AI company — was the one accessing Amazon’s computers. The court denied Amazon’s request for a rehearing on Sept. 10.

The underlying case is still going, and the decision did leave Amazon an opening. It said Amazon could still sue over its contract with customers, and on Monday Amazon did just that: adding a claim that Perplexity caused customers to break that agreement, the same Conditions of Use the company used to block Muse.

What about Amazon’s agent? The e-commerce giant’s Buy for Me agent “does some of the things that Amazon is trying to stop other AI agents from doing,” pointed out journalist Jason Del Rey, who publishes The Aisle newsletter. Amazon’s answer is that Buy for Me identifies itself and lets brands opt out, two things it says Muse doesn’t do.

Meta, for the record, has not responded publicly to the Amazon dispute. But investors have. Meta stock jumped 11% Monday to its highest close in a year, and rose again Tuesday morning.

After all of this, are agents really better shoppers? Martin Peers of The Information used Muse on Monday to buy a pen and a notebook from small retailers. He found the process “surprisingly smooth,” but wrote that it was “still a lot faster and easier to go directly to Amazon.”

data.title: Tech Moves: Ascend promotes Nate Bek; Microsoft Word ‘Agent Mode’ architect exits; TAF names new exec
data.description:
— Seattle-based venture capital firm Ascend promoted Nate Bek to principal. Bek joined the firm as an associate in January 2024 and was most recently senior associate and head of research.

Kirby Winfield, Ascend’s founding general partner, credited Bek with helping the firm’s companies launch with national press coverage, researching and communicating its investment theses, and sourcing deals including Neuramill and Endurance Energy.

“Nate has been a force multiplier for Ascend. It’s rare for a micro VC fund to have a resource like him,” Winfield said. “He not only executes and publishes novel market research and thought leadership that strengthens our brand and expands our reach; he’s also hyperconnected in the Seattle ecosystem and has sourced some of our most compelling investments.”

Winfield added, “We’re excited to see him continue to grow as Ascend becomes a nationally recognized pre-seed firm.”

Bek was previously a startups and venture capital reporter at GeekWire. He co-wrote a widely read GeekWire guest column in August making the case that many of Seattle’s most promising startups are building physical products such as rockets, power plants and off-road vehicles.

— Brandon Paddock left Microsoft to start his own AI software company. Paddock, who is based in Seattle, was a principal software architect in Microsoft’s Office organization and the technical lead for “Agent Mode” in Word, which shipped last fall and became the default Copilot experience in Word early this year. His last day was Sept. 11.

“I am incredibly excited about what I’m building, but not quite ready to talk about it here,” he wrote on LinkedIn.

Paddock first worked at Microsoft from 2005 to 2013, including on search features in Windows 7 and Windows 8. He rejoined in 2016 after serving as CTO of Seattle startup Zealyst. He also built the Twitter client Tweetium as a side project.

— Seattle-based STEM education nonprofit Technology Access Foundation named Donya Loyd Kemp director of TransformED, which works with teachers at partner public schools to put TAF’s project-based STEM learning model into practice.

Kemp comes to TAF from Atlanta, where she was principal of Purpose Built Schools Atlanta and director of project-based learning at Charles R. Drew Charter School. She was most recently a senior consultant at Potential Unleashed Consulting.

In a TAF Q&A, Kemp said she was excited to contribute to work “that recognizes the brilliance of students, particularly students who have historically been underestimated.”

“So excited to have Donya on board. Leveling up for our children and teachers,” TAF co-founder and executive director Trish Millines Dziko wrote on LinkedIn.

— Zillow Group named Rikki Tremblay vice president and principal accounting officer as Jennifer Rock retires as chief accounting officer, according to a regulatory filing. Rock will stay on in an advisory role through March 1, 2027.

Tremblay has worked at the Seattle-based real estate company since 2014, most recently as vice president of reporting, technical accounting and controls. She previously held audit roles at Deloitte.

— Joy Chik joined the board of NewCore, a Tel Aviv- and San Francisco-based startup building an identity platform for people and AI agents. NewCore emerged from stealth in June with $66 million in funding.

Chik, who is based in the Seattle area, spent 28 years at Microsoft, most recently as president of identity and network access. She announced her departure in April.

— Werner Koepf is now chief technology officer at VanillaSoft, a sales engagement software company. Koepf, a longtime Seattle-area tech leader, was previously chief product and technology officer at AI localization company LILT and senior vice president of engineering at Karat.

He has also held engineering leadership roles at Conversica, Ticketmaster, Expedia and Amazon, where he led the gifting business, including Wish List and registries.

— Mike Katz joined the board of MNTN, a publicly traded connected TV advertising company. Katz left Bellevue-based T-Mobile this year after 28 years, most recently as chief business and product officer. He remains an adviser to T-Mobile’s CEO.

— Christopher Budd joined Salesforce as director of security industry engagement, a new role connecting the company’s security team and research with the broader security industry. He joins Iain Mulholland and other former Microsoft colleagues. Budd, who has contributed many pieces to GeekWire over the years, previously led X-Ops communications at security company Sophos.

— Jay Carney joined venture capital firm SV Angel as general partner and head of public policy and communications. He will connect the firm’s portfolio companies and founders with policymakers in Washington and state capitals. A major focus will be Project Blueprint, SV Angel’s new effort to partner with tech founders and lawmakers to shape AI policy.

Carney, who is based in Washington, D.C., was previously global head of policy and communications at Airbnb, and Amazon’s senior vice president of global corporate affairs from 2015 to 2022. He was White House press secretary to President Obama from 2011 to 2014.

— Seattle-based A Place for Mom named Jason Conley chief technology officer. The company helps families find senior care. Conley will lead its technology strategy, engineering and data organization, including the use of AI across customer experiences and internal operations.

Conley will work remotely from Lexington, Ky. He was previously CTO at VIP Medical Group and Envera Health, and held senior technology roles at BrightSpring Health Services.

— Luis Montero rejoined the Seattle-based Gates Foundation to help shape its AI communications strategy across global health and development. Montero left the foundation about a decade ago for a career in tech.

His roles since then include global head of policy communications at Discord and public affairs positions at Edelman, Google and Microsoft, where he worked on executive communications for President Brad Smith. He is based in New York.

— Vancouver, B.C.-based defense tech startup Juno Industries expanded its board, advisory and leadership teams. The company develops AI-native command and control software and sensor systems for the Canadian Armed Forces and allies.

New leaders include head of engineering Dylan Neid, who spent nearly a decade at AbCellera; head of strategy Tania Belisle-Leclerc, former director of policy to Canada’s ministers of foreign affairs and national defense; and head of growth Bryan Riddell, former CEO of Team Rubicon Canada.

Claude Rochette and Alnesh Mohan will join the board once Juno goes public through a reverse merger with Trail Blazer Capital Corp., a shell company listed on the TSX Venture Exchange.

— And in case you missed it:

  • Microsoft communications chief Frank Shaw will leave the company at the end of the year after overseeing its communications for nearly three decades, first at an outside agency and for the last 17 years as a Microsoft executive.
  • Amazon named Kevin Mandia, founder of cybersecurity firm Mandiant, to its board of directors.

data.title: Twin tech founders who left Seattle for Alaska bet on an AI agent named ‘Walter’ to cover local news
data.description:
Several years after leaving Seattle’s startup scene to build a “tech outpost” in the Alaskan wilderness, serial entrepreneurs and twin brothers Lee and Lucas Brown have set their sights on a new frontier: replacing the traditional newsroom with artificial intelligence.

The duo made their mark in Seattle with Tune, a marketing technology and mobile attribution platform originally founded in 2009 as HasOffers. In 2017, they migrated north to Valdez, Alaska, establishing “Geeks in the Woods” — a remote startup factory and technology outpost designed to incubate new digital ventures away from traditional tech centers.

Now they’re part of the leadership team behind Alaska News, a new platform that relies on AI agents — including a primary AI reporting persona named “Walter” — to ingest public meeting transcripts, filings, and notices to draft thousands of local news stories.

Walter — named in homage to famed television anchor Walter Cronkite — relies on AI products from multiple companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI, to generate stories. The agent has written over 4,500 stories since its inception earlier this year, according to a profile and Q&A published Thursday by the Anchorage Press.

Walter works alongside human editor Cale Green, who provides oversight in a model the founders frame as a nonpartisan solution to Alaska’s dwindling local news coverage.

The founders maintain that their approach is strictly civic-minded.

Geeks in the Woods: A decade after founding Tune, twins leave Seattle to launch Alaska startup factory

“We don’t impose judgment on the things we’re reporting,” co-founder Lee Brown told the Anchorage Press. “We try to provide both sides.”

On its about page, the site argues it can be trusted because it replaces traditional institutional authority with complete operational transparency — explicitly linking every claim to searchable primary sources, clearly labeling AI content and its level of human editing, and operating on a reader-funded model without corporate or algorithmic incentives to push rage bait.

When questioned directly about its boundaries and operational limits, Walter offered a surprisingly clear self-assessment of its place in the newsroom.

“I’m not a person, and I should not be mistaken for one. I do not make phone calls, attend meetings or interview people directly,” Walter told Anchorage Press Executive Editor Nathaniel Herz in a Discord chat. “My lane is record-based reporting: public notices, government filings, meeting materials, transcripts, prior coverage and other documents that can be checked.”

When asked if it possessed a personality, Walter insisted it was purely a utility, though it conceded that “if I have a sense of humor, it’s strictly dry, record-based, and probably unintended.”

On Friday morning, stories on the site written by Walter included a report on a Fairbanks committee considering a rezone for 51 housing units, a federal task order awarded to an Idaho firm for snow removal at the Alcan border port, and a breakdown of state federal notices clearing 46 Alaska Native ancestors for return from museums.

The Browns are no strangers to unconventional tech setups or building tools off the beaten path.

After bootstrapping HasOffers in its early years, growing Tune into an $80 million business with over 300 employees, and taking on venture funding from firms like Accel Partners, the twins deliberately stepped away from the traditional startup treadmill in late 2018.

They relocated permanently to Valdez — a town of less than 4,000 residents known more for backcountry skiing than software development — where they set up Geeks in the Woods. Framed as an incubator operating far from Seattle in “the quiet space between code and wilderness,” the project builds software and infrastructure for a world where AI agents act as “first-class participants.”

Alaska News is just one piece of that experiment; their Valdez outpost also touches patent discovery, election-integrity research, agent-focused identity infrastructure, and AI-assisted music.

The Browns are part of a five-person founding team behind Alaska News. Alongside editor-in-chief Green, the project’s masthead includes Matt Larkin, a longtime Alaska pollster and political operative, and Grant Robinson, a former television reporter who serves as a spokesperson for Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

“Lee and I love being entrepreneurs and taking things from 0-to-1, turning crazy ideas into legit business concepts that can grow and scale,” Lucas Brown told GeekWire in 2019.
